text: The Taliban has published a biography of its reclusive founder, Mullah Mohammed Omar, asserting that he remains its leader. Afghan observers say the document aims to counter rumors of his death and reaffirm his authority as ISIS draws militant attention. Omar has not been seen or heard from in years.

Hundreds mourned Walter Scott at a South Carolina funeral Saturday, calling his death a catalyst for change. Scott was shot in the back while fleeing a police officer after a traffic stop; the officer has been fired and charged with murder.

A former TSA employee was sentenced to six months in jail for secretly filming a female co-worker in a restroom and entering her home to collect images and data. Daniel Boykin pleaded guilty to unlawful photography, aggravated burglary and a computer crime; he also faces five and a half years of probation.

Cape Verde is promoting its rich musical heritage to boost tourism and economic growth in a country with few conventional natural resources. Its Kriol Jazz Festival draws visitors, while the Atlantic Music Expo helps local artists reach international audiences.

Arsenal beat Burnley 1-0 on Aaron Ramsey’s first-half goal, moving within four points of Premier League leaders Chelsea, who have two games in hand. Elsewhere, Aston Villa and Leicester earned wins in the relegation fight, while Sunderland lost 4-1 to Crystal Palace.

Original *Twin Peaks* cast members have launched a #SaveTwinPeaks video campaign backing David Lynch amid his pay dispute with Showtime. Lynch says he is leaving the planned nine-episode revival because the budget is insufficient; Showtime says it still hopes to bring him back.

Andrew Getty, 47, grandson of oil tycoon J. Paul Getty, was found dead at his Los Angeles home. Authorities said the death appears to be from natural causes, with no signs of foul play; an autopsy is planned.

Maryland police arrested Nyia Parler after Philadelphia police said she left her 21-year-old quadriplegic son in a park for more than four days. He was found dehydrated and malnourished. Parler faces assault and other charges in Philadelphia, but her extradition must await completion of an unspecified treatment.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer has named an asteroid after Malala Yousafzai, the Nobel Peace Prize-winning Pakistani education activist. The dark, 4-kilometer-wide asteroid orbits the sun between Mars and Jupiter every five and a half years.

A gastrointestinal illness has sickened 95 passengers and five crew members aboard the Celebrity Infinity, the CDC said. The cause is unknown; CDC staff are due to meet the ship in San Diego on Monday.

The “Star Wars” saga’s digital HD release, Mindy Kaling’s brother’s claim that he posed as black to enter medical school, and the death of “Dukes of Hazzard” actor James Best were among the week’s trending stories. Other highlights included Burger King offering a free wedding to Joel Burger and Ashley King, Michelle Obama dancing at the White House Easter egg roll, and Nina Dobrev’s departure from “The Vampire Diaries.”

The FBI charged a Philadelphia woman with trying to travel overseas to fight for ISIS, citing social media posts and travel bookings. Two New York women were arrested the same day on charges of plotting to build a bomb for attacks in the United States.

HBO released a teaser for the second season of “True Detective,” which premieres June 21. Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams and Taylor Kitsch star in a California-set murder investigation involving conspiracy and betrayal.

Authorities charged Carlos Colina, 32, after human remains were found in a duffel bag and an apartment building common area in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The victim was identified as Jonathan Camilien, 26, who knew Colina. Investigators are awaiting medical examiner findings to determine whether additional charges are warranted.

Eastern High School basketball recruit Trey Moses asked freshman Ellie Meredith, who has Down syndrome, to be his prom date at their Louisville, Kentucky, school. The invitation, made during Ellie's P.E. class with flowers and a Taylor Swift-themed poster, drew widespread attention after a teacher posted photos online.

NBC’s “A.D. The Bible Continues” and the final episodes of AMC’s “Mad Men” lead this week’s TV picks. Other highlights include “American Odyssey,” returning comedy “Louie,” new series “The Comedians” and Netflix’s “Marvel’s Daredevil.”

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence faces a backlash over a religious freedom law critics say could permit discrimination against gay people. The controversy could push Republican presidential hopefuls to take harder-line positions on LGBT rights as similar bills advance in other states.

Apple’s latest mobile software update adds emojis with a range of skin tones, same-sex couples and more national flags. The expanded lineup has drawn praise for its inclusiveness and criticism from groups still left out, including redheads and Armenians.

Canadian singer Avril Lavigne said Lyme disease left her bedridden for five months, explaining her absence from the music scene. She says she is now “80 percent better” and plans to release a single this month in support of the 2015 Special Olympics.

New research by the Anne Frank House suggests Anne Frank and her sister Margot died of typhus at Bergen-Belsen at least a month earlier than the previously accepted March 1945 date. Their exact dates of death remain unknown.

Two Troy University students were arrested and charged with sexually assaulting a woman during spring break in Panama City Beach, Florida, authorities said. Investigators found video of the alleged attack, and the university suspended both students. Authorities said more arrests are expected.

A stray dog in Washington state survived being hit by a car, reportedly struck with a hammer and buried, then reached a farm four days later. The dog, now named Theia, is receiving veterinary care for serious injuries; donations have surpassed $10,000 to help pay for treatment.

The FBI confirmed that Malaysian bomb maker Marwan was killed in a January raid in the southern Philippines. The operation left 44 police commandos dead and raised concerns about a fragile peace agreement with Muslim rebels.

A U.S. lawmaker argues that the proposed Iran nuclear framework gives Tehran sanctions relief while allowing it to retain much of its nuclear infrastructure. He urges tougher, longer-lasting restrictions and inspections to guard against a secret weapons program.

“Mad Men” begins its final episodes Sunday, ending an eight-year run that made the 1960s advertising drama a cultural touchstone. With its characters facing upheaval after the 1969 moon landing, the article speculates about how Don Draper and his colleagues might part ways.

Katie, a giraffe at the Dallas Zoo, gave birth to a calf about 6 feet tall Friday evening during an hour-long labor streamed live online. The calf was seen moving its ears, trying to stand and attempting to nurse; its sex and condition were not immediately announced.

Loretta Lynch’s nomination to become the first African-American woman attorney general has waited longer for a full Senate vote after clearing committee than any recent nominee. Supporters say race may be a factor; Senate Republicans deny that and cite partisan disputes over immigration and a human trafficking bill.

Armed assailants stormed the attorney general’s office in Afghanistan’s northern Balkh province Thursday, killing three security personnel and wounding five people, officials said. Most staff and civilians were rescued, but fighting with Afghan security forces continued.

Bob Barker returned to host part of the April 1 episode of “The Price Is Right,” eight years after stepping down. The 91-year-old led the “Lucky Seven” game before handing the show back to Drew Carey.
Blues legend B.B. King, 89, was hospitalized for dehydration linked to his Type II diabetes. He said Tuesday he was feeling much better and had returned home to rest.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all counts in the Boston Marathon bombing. A CNN opinion writer argues that extremists exploit young Muslims’ grievances and that engaged Muslim communities can offer alternatives to violence.

CNN’s videos of the week include a tour of Mike Tyson’s abandoned Ohio mansion, a ride on a record-setting roller coaster and an interview about sexual assault allegations against Bikram yoga creator Bikram Choudhury. Other clips cover a witness to the Germanwings crash, a debate over Indiana’s religious freedom law and a study of facial attractiveness.

Coalition forces have retaken 25-30% of the Iraqi territory seized by ISIS, the Pentagon says. A counterinsurgency expert cautioned that the gains are mainly along the group’s front lines and that ISIS may stage attacks elsewhere to offset losses and sustain its image.

A passenger tried to choke Ottawa Fury soccer player Oliver Minatel with a headphone cord aboard an Air Canada flight from Toronto to Atlanta, witnesses said. Other passengers intervened, and authorities escorted the suspect off the plane after landing. He was taken for a medical and mental evaluation; no federal charges were pending.

A Hong Kong court adjourned until May a hearing to determine whether former banker Rurik Jutting should stand trial for the murders of two Indonesian women. Police found the women’s bodies in his Wan Chai apartment last November; more than 200 pieces of forensic and DNA evidence remain under analysis.

Tornadoes tore through the rural Midwest on Thursday, killing one person in Fairdale, Illinois, and damaging dozens of homes near Rochelle. Officials said warnings likely saved lives as responders searched damaged areas for trapped residents.
Don McLean’s 16-page manuscript for “American Pie” sold for $1.2 million at a Christie’s auction Tuesday. The draft includes unused lyrics and notes on the 1972 hit.

The head of the U.N. agency for Palestinian refugees will visit Syria’s Yarmouk camp Saturday to assess conditions for the 18,000 civilians still there, including 3,500 children. The camp has been largely cut off from aid since 2013 amid fighting and reported shortages of food and medical care.

Saudi-led airstrikes have damaged targets in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, but Houthi rebels remain in control. Nearly 600 people have been killed in fighting across the country, while power outages and delayed medical supplies have deepened the humanitarian crisis.

Richie Benaud, the former Australia cricket captain who became one of the sport’s most celebrated broadcasters, has died aged 84. He played 64 Tests and never lost a series as captain. Tributes came from cricket figures and political leaders around the world.

A total lunar eclipse will be visible across western North America this morning, with totality lasting just four minutes and 43 seconds—the shortest of the century, NASA says. Partial views will be possible elsewhere in the United States, though sunrise will cut the display short on the East Coast.

A federal grand jury charged real estate heir Robert Durst, 71, with unlawfully possessing a revolver found in his New Orleans hotel room. Durst is being held without bail and awaits extradition to Los Angeles to face a first-degree murder charge in the 2000 killing of his friend Susan Berman.

“Furious 7” opens Friday as a tribute to Paul Walker, who died in a car crash during production. His brothers served as body doubles to complete scenes, and the film retires his character rather than killing him off.

A “Price Is Right” model accidentally revealed the winning answer in a car giveaway, handing a contestant a new Hyundai Sonata. Host Drew Carey laughed off the mistake, and model Manuela Arbelaez later said everything turned out OK.

Thai Smile has unveiled an “Adventure Time”-themed Airbus A320, with characters from the Cartoon Network show featured inside and out. The plane’s first flight is scheduled for April 4, from Bangkok to Phuket.
Pedestrians stopped traffic on a busy Washington street Tuesday to help a mother duck and her ducklings cross safely. They then guided the birds to a nearby grassy area.

French investigators have collected the main evidence from the Alpine site where Germanwings Flight 9525 crashed, killing all 150 people aboard. Both flight recorders have been recovered, and investigators say initial data shows co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately accelerated the plane’s descent.

Cuba is attending the Summit of the Americas for the first time after the U.S. dropped its opposition, offering a chance to advance talks on reopening embassies. Havana says it must first be removed from the U.S. terrorism list, while its support for Venezuela could complicate the diplomatic thaw.

Jesus and his disciples likely lived at a subsistence level, relying on hospitality and donations to support their travels. The Gospels identify women including Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna as financial supporters of the ministry.

California regulators ordered Pacific Gas & Electric to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty for unsafe gas pipeline operations, including a 2010 San Bruno explosion that killed eight people. Most of the penalty will fund pipeline safety improvements.

Lauren Hill, 19, whose fight against brain cancer inspired people worldwide, died Friday. The Indiana basketball player fulfilled her dream of playing for Mount St. Joseph University after the NCAA moved up the team’s season opener. She also helped raise $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research.

A large fire broke out Friday morning at General Electric’s Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky, sending thick smoke over the area. Firefighters battled the blaze, which reached at least four alarms; no injuries were reported, and the cause was unknown.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif received a hero’s welcome after helping secure a framework nuclear deal that could lead to sanctions relief. Educated in the United States, he has worked closely with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry; negotiators now face a June 30 deadline to settle the details.

A Connecticut judge has denied a 17-year-old’s request to return home or receive visitors while she remains in state custody for chemotherapy to treat Hodgkin lymphoma. The teen is in remission, and her lawyers are considering an appeal. Her treatment is expected to end in April, after which she is expected to be allowed home.

A computer analysis of word choices and phrasing suggests Shakespeare wrote much of “Double Falsehood,” with John Fletcher contributing to its second half. The play was published by Lewis Theobald in 1728, but its authorship remains disputed.

French investigators said they had not seen a purported cellphone video of the final moments of Germanwings Flight 9525, despite reports by two magazines that they had viewed it. Lufthansa confirmed that co-pilot Andreas Lubitz, suspected of deliberately crashing the plane and killing all 150 aboard, had disclosed a past episode of severe depression during training.

American Samoan veteran Emy Afalava is challenging the federal government’s refusal to recognize people born in the U.S. territory as citizens. A ruling from the D.C. Circuit could come soon in a case the article links to a history of unequal treatment of island territories.

Blue Bell has temporarily closed its Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, plant after listeria was found in ice cream made there. The CDC warned consumers not to eat products from that plant, while investigators examine possible links to illnesses in Kansas and Texas.

Al-Shabaab has claimed an attack on Kenya’s Garissa University College that killed many people and left others hostage. The assault reflects the group’s expanding cross-border campaign and deepening insecurity in East Africa. Lasting stability will require addressing political and economic exclusion alongside military action, the article argues.

The United States said a Russian fighter jet intercepted a U.S. reconnaissance plane over the Baltic Sea on Tuesday with unsafe, aggressive maneuvers. Washington plans to lodge a diplomatic complaint; Russia said its pilot was identifying the aircraft, which it claimed had its transponder off.

A black-winged angel painted by North Charleston artist Phillip Hyman has become a symbol at Black Lives Matter protests after the police shooting of Walter Scott. Hyman says he made the piece to mourn with Scott’s family.

Bystander video of North Charleston Officer Michael Slager fatally shooting Walter Scott as he ran away has raised questions about initial police accounts that Scott took Slager’s Taser. Slager has been fired and charged with murder; an independent state agency is investigating.

ISIS claimed Sunday that its fighters had seized several buildings at Iraq’s Baiji oil refinery after an assault. Iraqi officials denied the claim, saying government forces remained in full control; CNN could not independently verify either account.

Nashville’s district attorney has barred prosecutors from offering female sterilization in plea deals after public outrage over the practice. A CNN legal analysis says such deals may be constitutional and argues that the reaction exposes a double standard: sterilization of male offenders has drawn far less scrutiny.

The Ebola epidemic has infected more than 25,000 people and killed more than 10,000. New cases have fallen to their lowest weekly level since May 2014, but undetected transmission in Guinea threatens efforts to end the outbreak.

The NCAA says it has no legal duty to ensure the quality of athletes’ education, responding to a lawsuit by former University of North Carolina athletes over fraudulent classes. Critics say the position contradicts the NCAA’s longstanding claim that education is central to college sports.

An explosion at a controversial chemical plant in China’s Fujian province injured six people and sparked a large fire, authorities said. More than 600 firefighters brought the blaze under control; local media reported no toxic chemical spill.

Bystander video of a North Charleston officer shooting Walter Scott as he fled underscores the need for police body cameras, a defense attorney argues. The cameras could deter excessive force and help restore public trust, though addressing racial bias in policing will require broader reforms.

A meeting between Barack Obama and Raúl Castro was expected to dominate the Summit of the Americas in Panama. But U.S. sanctions on Venezuelan officials have drawn protests from President Nicolás Maduro and support for him from Cuba, raising tensions ahead of the gathering.

A Russian nuclear submarine caught fire while undergoing repairs at a shipyard in northwestern Russia, state media reported. Officials said the reactor fuel and ammunition had been removed, no one was injured and the fire posed no threat to the shipyard.

Tropical storm Maysak weakened from a super typhoon as it approached the Philippines on Saturday, but authorities warned of flash floods and landslides. Precautionary evacuations and outdoor activity bans were in place ahead of its expected landfall in Isabela province Sunday morning.

NFL legend Deion Sanders called out his son on Twitter for claiming he only eats “hood doughnuts,” pointing to the younger Sanders’ trust fund, condo and clothing line. Deion Sanders Jr., a wide receiver at Southern Methodist University, retweeted his father’s remarks.

Violence against women remains widespread in Guatemala, where two women are killed daily and most homicide cases never reach court. Survivor Adelma Cifuentes won a conviction against her abusive husband and now uses theater to help others, while rights groups and the government pursue broader reforms.

Police in Malegaon, India, are requiring owners to submit photographs and identifying details of their cattle to help enforce Maharashtra’s beef ban. More than 100 owners have complied, while beef traders have vowed to challenge the law in court.

Police in Lucknow, India, have bought four camera-equipped drones that can spray pepper at violent crowds and plan to buy a fifth. Critics say the tactic needs regulation and could suppress protests rather than address them through dialogue.

Don McLean’s 16-page handwritten lyrics for “American Pie” sold at Christie’s on Tuesday for $1.2 million to an unnamed buyer. The 1971 song, inspired in part by the plane crash that killed Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and the Big Bopper, remains a widely interpreted pop anthem.

A gang broke into safety deposit boxes in London’s Hatton Garden jewelry district over Easter weekend in a rare, meticulously planned heist. A former Scotland Yard commander says detectives will examine possible inside involvement, forensic evidence and CCTV footage as they trace the thieves and stolen goods.
7-Eleven will hold its first U.S. Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day on Saturday, offering fills for $1.49 at participating stores. Containers must be sanitary and fit through a 10-inch opening.

Former Kentucky state senator Georgia Davis Powers criticized Rand Paul’s presidential campaign launch, saying his pledge to broaden Republican appeal is at odds with his record. She cited his comments on civil rights and voting rights, as well as his positions on education, abortion and immigration.

A passenger died Sunday when a Lamborghini crashed into a guardrail at the Exotic Driving Experience at Walt Disney World Speedway. Florida Highway Patrol said the driver lost control and suffered minor injuries.

The defense rested Monday in former NFL player Aaron Hernandez’s trial for the 2013 killing of Odin Lloyd, calling its witnesses in less than a day. Jurors are expected to begin deliberating after Tuesday’s closing arguments in a case built largely on circumstantial evidence. Hernandez has pleaded not guilty.

Chinese authorities detained Wu Rongrong and four other women’s rights activists over a planned protest against sexual harassment. They face release or formal arrest by April 13, amid a broader crackdown on independent activism that contrasts with Beijing’s stated commitment to women’s rights.

Former Maryland Gov. Martin O’Malley said in Iowa that Hillary Clinton’s lead in the Democratic presidential race does not make her nomination inevitable. The potential contender called for a competitive primary as Clinton prepared to launch her campaign.

Former NFL player Aaron Hernandez was convicted Wednesday of murdering Odin Lloyd in 2013 and sentenced to life in prison. Lloyd’s family described him in court as a devoted son and brother; his mother said she forgave those involved in his death.

Republican presidential candidate Ted Cruz is courting Iowa’s evangelical voters, defending religious liberty and emphasizing his Christian faith. He hopes to pair their support with tea party and libertarian voters, but faces a crowded field that includes past Iowa winners Mike Huckabee and Rick Santorum.

Marvel unveiled Paul Bettany as the Vision in a new “Avengers: Age of Ultron” poster and showed Charlie Cox’s red “Daredevil” suit ahead of the Netflix series. New images also revealed Ben Hardy as Angel in “X-Men: Apocalypse” and Jamie Bell as the Thing in the “Fantastic Four” reboot.

The Italian Coast Guard rescued 978 migrants in the Mediterranean off Libya on Friday. More than 10,000 migrants arrived in Italy in the first three months of 2015, while at least 480 died trying to cross the sea.

French-language broadcaster TV5Monde was gradually restoring service Thursday after a cyberattack disrupted its 11 channels, website and social media accounts. ISIS markings appeared on its accounts, but no group immediately claimed responsibility.

David Lynch says he will not direct Showtime’s planned “Twin Peaks” revival, citing insufficient funding to make it as he envisioned. Showtime says it hopes to resolve the dispute and bring back the series with Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost.

Jurors began deliberating in the Boston Marathon bombing trial Tuesday, while closing arguments were set in former NFL player Aaron Hernandez’s murder trial. Sen. Rand Paul announced a presidential bid, and voters went to the polls in Chicago’s mayoral runoff and Ferguson’s City Council election.

Tornadoes were reported across Kansas on Wednesday night, including one near Wichita that moved away from the city. A possible tornado, flooding and hail were also reported in Missouri. More storms were forecast across the central United States on Thursday.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of release for the 2008 murder of her ex-boyfriend, Travis Alexander. The judge imposed the sentence after two juries failed to agree on whether Arias should receive the death penalty.

The EPA found methyl bromide in a U.S. Virgin Islands villa where a Delaware family of four fell ill and was hospitalized. Officials are investigating whether a nearby fumigation caused the illness, while the Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation.

A Columbia Journalism School review found widespread reporting and editing failures in Rolling Stone’s discredited University of Virginia rape story. UVA cannot sue for defamation, but members of the fraternity named in the article may have a case if they can show the story implicated them and caused measurable harm.

FBI agents shot and wounded a suspect linked to 32 commercial robberies after confronting him outside a Georgia CVS on Saturday. Two agents were injured in vehicle collisions as the suspect tried to flee; both were treated and released.

An Alaska Airlines flight returned to Seattle shortly after takeoff when the pilot heard banging from the cargo hold. A baggage handler who said he had fallen asleep inside was taken to a hospital as a precaution and discharged. The airline is investigating.

A North Carolina judge ruled that Craig Hicks can face the death penalty in the February shootings of three Muslim college students in Chapel Hill. Hicks is charged with three counts of first-degree murder. Authorities have cited a possible parking dispute and are also examining whether the killings were a hate crime.

Amnesty International says women’s rights activists in Afghanistan face attacks from militants, warlords and officials, while authorities often ignore threats and fail to protect them. The killing of Farkhunda in Kabul sparked protests, with women carrying her coffin in a rare public show of defiance.

A New York judge has allowed a woman to serve divorce papers on her husband through a private Facebook message. The ruling highlights how online service may offer a more reliable way to notify people who cannot be reached in person.

The Rev. Robert H. Schuller, founder of the “Hour of Power” television ministry and California’s Crystal Cathedral, has died at 88, his family said. His upbeat preaching drew millions of viewers, but his ministry later struggled with family disputes, falling donations and bankruptcy.

Four workers died and 45 were injured in a fire on a Pemex oil platform off Mexico’s coast Wednesday. About 300 people were evacuated before crews extinguished the blaze that night. Pemex said there was no oil spill; the cause remains unknown.

Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback signed the nation’s first law banning a common second-trimester abortion procedure, with an exception to protect the mother’s life or health. Supporters hailed it as a model for other states; opponents said it endangers women and vowed to fight it.

Chinese state television host Bi Fujian apologized after a video showed him cursing Mao Zedong while singing at a dinner party. CCTV said it would investigate, as the clip sparked debate online over his remarks and the private setting.

Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized after a hot mic caught him using a racial slur about Wisconsin’s Frank Kaminsky following Kentucky’s loss Saturday. Harrison said he meant no disrespect; Kaminsky said they had spoken and he was “over it.”

“Arrested Development” executive producer Brian Grazer says the comedy will return for a fifth season of 17 episodes. Netflix has not confirmed the plans, and it is unclear whether the full cast will return.

CERN restarted the Large Hadron Collider on Sunday, circulating its first beams after a two-year shutdown and a delay in March. Scientists plan to raise the beams to record energy levels to probe unanswered questions about the universe, including dark matter and the origin of mass.

An Iranian observation plane flew within 50 yards of a U.S. Navy helicopter over the Persian Gulf this month, U.S. officials told CNN. No shots were fired, but the encounter raised concerns about the risk of escalation and whether local Iranian forces were acting without orders from senior commanders.

A jury found Dzhokhar Tsarnaev guilty on all 30 counts in the Boston Marathon bombing trial, including 17 capital charges. The case now moves to a penalty phase in which jurors will decide whether he receives the death penalty.

Police arrested four employees of Indian retailer FabIndia after a minister spotted a camera overlooking a changing room at a Goa store. Authorities said the camera could photograph customers inside; the employees face voyeurism and privacy charges.

Iran plans to allow women and families into some sports stadiums within the next year, a deputy sports minister said, though it remains unclear which events will be covered. Women have been barred from most men’s sporting events since the 1979 revolution, a policy that has drawn international criticism.

An Indian court sentenced Satyam founder Ramalinga Raju and nine others to seven years in jail over a $1.6 billion accounting fraud. Raju, who admitted inflating the software firm’s profits with fictitious assets and cash, was also fined $804,000.

Alaska Airlines removed cancer patient Elizabeth Sedway from a flight from Hawaii after she said she sometimes felt weak and could not provide a doctor’s note. She flew home to California the next day; the airline apologized, refunded her family’s tickets and paid for their overnight stay.

Kayahan, one of Turkey’s best-loved singers and songwriters, died of cancer Friday in Istanbul at 66. Known for his love songs, he rose to prominence after competing in the 1990 Eurovision Song Contest and releasing his hit album “I Made a Vow” the following year.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called the proposed Iran nuclear deal “a very bad deal” and urged world powers to increase pressure for tougher terms. U.S. officials defended the framework as a way to curb Iran’s nuclear program, while lawmakers remained divided.

A suspected domestic kidnapping led to connected shootings near the U.S. Census Bureau in Maryland and on Washington’s H Street, police said. A security guard was critically wounded; the suspect and an officer were also wounded after a chase and shootout. The kidnapping victim was found in good condition.

Imprisoned former U.S. Army analyst Chelsea Manning has joined Twitter, dictating posts by phone to a firm because she cannot access the Internet in prison. Manning is serving a 35-year sentence for leaking classified documents to WikiLeaks.

Rapper Nelly was arrested on drug charges Saturday after Tennessee troopers stopped and searched his tour bus. Authorities said they found methamphetamine, marijuana, drug paraphernalia and several handguns. Nelly later posted bond and was released.

A Delaware father is improving, but his two teenage sons remain in critical condition after the family fell ill at a U.S. Virgin Islands villa. The EPA found methyl bromide in their unit and is investigating whether a nearby pest treatment caused the illnesses; the Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation.

Online journalists across Asia face growing legal pressure as governments restrict dissent outside tightly controlled traditional media. Recent arrests in Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam highlight the risks, while killings of bloggers in Bangladesh show the deadly threat posed by attackers who often escape punishment.

Nina Dobrev says she will leave “The Vampire Diaries” at the end of its sixth season, though the CW show will return for a seventh. Fans questioned whether it should continue without her and worried about the fate of her character’s romance with Damon Salvatore.

ISIS’s assault on Yarmouk has intensified fighting in the besieged Palestinian district near Damascus, where residents report Syrian government bombing and shelling. About 18,000 people remain, many without adequate food, water or medical care, while aid access is severely restricted.

Astronomers estimate the Milky Way may contain billions of rocky planets where liquid water could exist. NASA plans to search for signs of life on exoplanets and closer to home, but communication with intelligent aliens remains unlikely given the vast distances and uncertain lifespans of civilizations.

Carlos Colina, 32, faces a murder charge after the remains of Jonathan Camilien, 26, were found in a duffel bag and at an apartment building in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Authorities said the two men knew each other.

Kanye West has settled a lawsuit brought by photographer Daniel Ramos over a 2013 scuffle at Los Angeles International Airport. West apologized to Ramos, and the two shook hands; settlement terms were not disclosed.

A CNN opinion writer argues that President Barack Obama’s political stake in an Iran nuclear deal weakened the U.S. negotiating position. The writer says the proposed framework leaves much of Iran’s nuclear infrastructure intact and could heighten fears of proliferation and instability in the Middle East.

Video of a North Charleston officer fatally shooting Walter Scott led to the officer’s arrest on murder charges and contradicted his initial account. The case highlights a national gap in police-use-of-force data despite a 1994 federal law requiring its collection, prompting calls for comprehensive reporting.

Five American clinicians exposed to Ebola in Sierra Leone were released after three weeks of monitoring at a Nebraska hospital; none developed the disease. A colleague diagnosed with Ebola remains in fair condition at the National Institutes of Health.

Mark Ronson’s “Uptown Funk!,” featuring Bruno Mars, topped the Billboard Hot 100 for a 13th week, the longest run at No. 1 of any song in the 2010s. Natalie La Rose entered the top 10 for the first time with “Somebody,” featuring Jeremih.

Fans marked April 8 as “Rex Manning Day,” a nod to the 1995 film “Empire Records,” while “Lost” fans celebrated the date’s significance to their show. Other movie dates include April 25 from “Miss Congeniality,” October 3 from “Mean Girls” and October 21, 2015, from “Back to the Future Part II.”

“Grace of Monaco,” starring Nicole Kidman, will premiere on Lifetime on May 25 instead of opening in U.S. theaters. The Weinstein Co. sold the critically panned film to the network after poor international results and a dispute over its final cut.

Tokyo’s Shibuya ward passed an ordinance to issue partnership certificates to same-sex couples, enabling hospital visitation and joint tenancy agreements. The certificates, expected this summer, will not be legally binding, but advocates called the move a step toward marriage equality in Japan.

California’s fourth year of drought has prompted a mandatory 25% cut in urban water use and could raise food prices nationwide. Grocery prices have already risen for some produce, while drought across the West has pushed up beef prices. The impact on this year’s harvests remains uncertain.

The University of Michigan will screen “American Sniper” after reversing a decision to cancel it over student objections to its portrayal of the Middle East. A university official said the cancellation conflicted with its commitment to freedom of expression; an alternative screening of “Paddington” will also be offered.

Amy Schumer’s opener, Channing Tatum’s onstage twerk and musical performances were among Billboard’s highlights of the 2015 MTV Movie Awards. Its misfires included a botched archery gag, an awkward “Gone Girl” joke and several flat presenter bits.

A boat fragment suspected to be debris from Japan’s 2011 tsunami was towed into Newport, Oregon, with yellowtail jack fish native to Japanese waters inside. Biologists said the risk from invasive species was small; the fish will go to an aquarium, and the debris to a landfill.

More than 200 Nigerian schoolgirls remain missing a year after Boko Haram abducted them from a school in Chibok. President-elect Muhammadu Buhari pledged to fight the militants, as families and supporters renewed calls for the girls’ return.

A CNN commentary explains the Easter Triduum as the progression from Jesus’ crucifixion on Good Friday, through the uncertainty of Holy Saturday, to the resurrection on Easter Sunday. It argues that the sequence mirrors recurring human experiences of suffering, waiting and renewal.

Kenya has frozen 86 accounts linked to suspected Al-Shabaab supporters after the militant group killed 147 people at a university in Garissa. As Kenyans mourned the victims, authorities faced criticism over delays in responding to the attack.

After his tech start-up was denied funding, Jia Jiang began a “100 Days of Rejection” project to confront his fear of hearing no. A video of a Krispy Kreme manager fulfilling one of his unusual requests went viral, and Jiang has since turned the experience into a book about treating rejection as an opportunity.

Attorney General Eric Holder reminded Justice Department employees that they are barred from soliciting or accepting commercial sex, even where prostitution is legal and while off duty. The memo followed a watchdog report on DEA agents’ misconduct overseas; violators face suspension or dismissal.

North Carolina authorities are investigating whether the fatal shooting of Wayne Community College employee Ron Lane was a hate crime. Suspect Kenneth Morgan Stancil III, a former work-study employee, was arrested Tuesday in Florida after fleeing the scene, police said.

Amnesty International says some governments used the death penalty in 2014 to respond to crime, terrorism and unrest, despite no evidence that executions deter crime more than prison. Recorded executions fell from 778 to 607, excluding China, where the figures are secret.

A Duke University student admitted hanging a noose near the student union, officials said. The student is no longer on campus and faces a conduct review, while a criminal investigation continues. Students and faculty rallied Wednesday to condemn the act.

Richard Dysart, who won an Emmy for playing senior partner Leland McKenzie on “L.A. Law,” has died at 86 after a long illness. His career also included the original Broadway production of “That Championship Season” and roles in “The Thing” and “Wall Street.”

Christians celebrated Easter with services at the Vatican and in Jerusalem, marking Jesus’ crucifixion and resurrection. The holiday’s shifting date is tied to the spring equinox and moon phases, while Orthodox Christians often observe it later under a different calendar. Easter eggs and the bunny have separate, less certain origins.
Comedian Chris Rock posted photos documenting three police traffic stops in seven weeks, renewing debate over racial profiling. He did not say why he was stopped or how the latest encounter ended.
Bob Burns, the original drummer for Lynyrd Skynyrd, died Friday night when his car struck a mailbox and tree in Georgia. He was 64. Burns helped form the band in 1965 and left in 1975.
A photo of a cat on a staircase has sparked a social media debate over whether it is going up or down. The image spread after appearing on 9GAG, drawing comparisons to the viral #TheDress illusion.

The United States and five other powers reached a framework deal with Iran in Lausanne to curb its nuclear program and expand inspections. The article argues that critics misstate the deal’s goals and terms, and warns that a congressional rejection could weaken sanctions and strain alliances.

Rolling Stone’s retraction of a discredited gang-rape story has not ended scrutiny of how the University of Virginia handles sexual assault allegations. UVA, which has never expelled a student for sexual assault, faces state and federal investigations. Survivors and advocates fear the retraction could discourage victims from coming forward.

Indiana Pacers forward Chris Copeland and a female companion were stabbed near a New York nightclub early Wednesday. Copeland was in stable condition; Atlanta Hawks players Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha, who police said were not involved in the stabbing, were arrested on obstruction and disorderly conduct charges.

Twisted Sister says its 2016 tour, marking the band’s 40th anniversary, will be its last. Mike Portnoy will replace drummer A.J. Pero, who died in March, and the band will play two shows in Pero’s honor.

John Travolta says he has not seen HBO’s critical Scientology documentary “Going Clear” and does not plan to. The actor says his 40 years with the church have been positive and credits it with helping him cope with his son’s death.

“Furious 7” opened to a record $146 million weekend as fans praised its emotional tribute to Paul Walker, who died before filming was complete. The film retires his character, Brian, with a family-focused farewell and a montage of Walker’s earlier scenes.

“Game of Thrones” returns Sunday for its fifth season, premiering simultaneously in 170 countries. Major storylines are expected to converge as the show moves beyond parts of George R.R. Martin’s books, with larger battles and unrest among ordinary people.

Five people survived days to more than a year adrift at sea after storms, equipment failures or a tsunami left them stranded. They endured by catching food, collecting rainwater or clinging to debris before being rescued or reaching land.
The first six “Star Wars” films arrive on digital HD Friday with behind-the-scenes extras. One feature shows how sound designer Ben Burtt created the Geonosians’ alien sounds.

A jury found Dzhokhar Tsarnaev guilty on all 30 counts stemming from the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing and its aftermath. Survivors and victims’ families welcomed the verdict as a step toward accountability, while saying it could not undo their losses.

Chinese prosecutors charged former security chief Zhou Yongkang with bribery, abuse of power and leaking state secrets. The former Politburo Standing Committee member is the highest-ranking official to face corruption charges under President Xi Jinping’s anti-graft campaign.

Philadelphia police say a mother left her 21-year-old son, who has cerebral palsy and is quadriplegic, in a park for more than four days while she visited her boyfriend in Maryland. He was hospitalized with dehydration, malnutrition and other injuries. The mother was arrested Sunday and faces assault, neglect and other charges.

Walmart’s opposition to an Arkansas religious freedom bill helped prompt the governor to demand changes amid warnings that it could enable discrimination against gay and lesbian people. The retailer’s stance, alongside a wider business backlash in Arkansas and Indiana, underscores shifting views on gay rights and puts pressure on Republicans.

A lapsed Catholic says Pope Francis’ welcoming tone has rekindled her faith after years of feeling rejected by the church. Cardinal Gerald Lacroix says the church should welcome everyone while maintaining its teachings.

Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau and Vili Fualaau say they remain happily married as they approach their 10th wedding anniversary. In an upcoming ABC interview, the former teacher, who served more than seven years in prison over their relationship when he was her student, discusses plans to teach again and seek removal from the sex offender registry.

Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential bid risks becoming a test of U.S. gender equality, a burden male candidates do not face, a CNN opinion piece argues. Its author says a win would not resolve broader inequities, while a loss should not be taken as proof that women cannot win major elections.

Amnesty International says governments used terrorism and security threats to justify executions in 2014, citing Pakistan and China. Recorded executions fell nearly 22% to at least 607, excluding China, while death sentences rose 28% to at least 2,466.

Japan’s defense minister told parliament that the Air Self Defense Force has never encountered a UFO believed to be from outer space. He was responding to a question from former wrestler and lawmaker Antonio Inoki about possible extraterrestrial threats.

Mark Wahlberg will star in and produce “Patriots’ Day,” a film about the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing and the ensuing manhunt, Deadline reported. The film is expected to be told from the perspective of former Boston Police Commissioner Ed Davis.

Martin O’Malley and Jim Webb, both long-shot contenders for the 2016 Democratic presidential nomination, showed contrasting styles at an Iowa dinner: O’Malley worked the room, while Webb stayed more reserved. Both trail Hillary Clinton badly in polls, though Webb pledged to campaign across Iowa.

Turkish authorities arrested nine British citizens, including four children, at the Turkey-Syria border Wednesday on suspicion of trying to cross illegally into Syria. Officials did not say why the group was attempting to enter the country.

The Justice Department has charged FedEx with shipping prescription drugs for illegal online pharmacies, alleging it continued after repeated warnings. FedEx denies wrongdoing and says common-carrier laws protect its routine deliveries. The case tests how far a courier’s liability extends when it knows shipments may be illegal.

Kenyans used the hashtag #147notjustanumber to share stories of those killed in the Al-Shabaab attack on Garissa University College. Churches mourned the 147 victims at Easter services under armed guard. Officials identified one slain attacker as the son of a Kenyan government official.

Swedish photographer Johan Bavman is documenting fathers who take extended parental leave, capturing both the rewards and exhaustion of caring for young children. Sweden offers parents 480 days of leave, including 60 reserved for fathers, but only 12% of couples divide the time equally.

President Barack Obama said the United States would help Israel maintain its military advantage and stand by it if attacked, as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu criticized the proposed Iran nuclear deal. Obama said the deal could prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon even if its leaders cannot be trusted.

Indiana’s new religious freedom law has sparked criticism that it could enable discrimination against gay people. Similar laws exist in 20 states, but legal claims under them are rare and have largely involved religious minorities. Cases over sacred eagle feathers, ceremonial tea, kosher meals and a Sikh kirpan show mixed outcomes.

Chinese police have recommended public-order charges against five feminists detained before planned International Women’s Day protests against sexual harassment. The charge carries up to five years in prison; prosecutors have until Monday to decide whether to pursue it. Their detention has drawn international criticism.

Selena’s family is developing “Selena the One,” a digital version of the Tejano star, 20 years after her death. The project aims to release new music and videos and tour in 2018, with an Indiegogo campaign seeking $500,000 for its launch.

Former U.S. Rep. Michele Bachmann compared President Barack Obama’s Iran nuclear negotiations to the Germanwings co-pilot accused of deliberately crashing a plane, killing 150 people. Her Facebook post drew criticism as inappropriate and disrespectful.

Ryan Gosling’s directorial debut, “Lost River,” has drawn mixed reviews, but its portrayal of Detroit’s decay has stood out. Gosling says the city’s threatened buildings inspired the film, which also reflects residents’ resilience and signs of renewal.
British police charged Yahya Rashid, 19, with terrorism offenses after arresting him at Luton airport on his return from Turkey. He is due to appear in a London court Wednesday.

Mötley Crüe singer Vince Neil’s national anthem performance before a Las Vegas Outlaws game drew criticism. The article contrasts it with Whitney Houston’s acclaimed rendition and recalls controversial versions by Roseanne Barr, Jimi Hendrix and Michael Bolton.

Nearly 2,000 World War I soldiers’ inscriptions have been found in an underground quarry near Naours, France, where troops took refuge close to the Somme battlefield. Photographer Jeff Gusky has documented 1,821 names, mostly Australian and British, offering a record of the men who passed through.

The Palestinian Authority became the 123rd member of the International Criminal Court, giving it jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories since June 2014. The court has opened a preliminary examination that could lead to investigations of suspects on both sides. Israel and the United States opposed the move.

Anthony Ray Hinton was freed Friday after nearly 30 years on Alabama’s death row when prosecutors dropped charges in two 1985 murders. A new trial had been ordered after firearms experts said the gun attributed to him could not be matched to evidence in either killing. Hinton, who maintained his innocence, called his imprisonment a miscarriage of justice.

Most U.S. taxpayers receive refunds, and easier filing makes Tax Day feel like a windfall, the author argues. That happy ending can obscure a tax system that favors income from capital over wages and penalizes some two-earner couples.

Jordan Spieth will take a four-shot lead into the final round of the 2015 Masters despite a late double bogey on Saturday. Justin Rose is second at 12 under, with Phil Mickelson at 11 under; Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy are at six under.

A New York woman who married 10 men pleaded not guilty to charges that she falsely called her 2010 marriage her first and only one. Prosecutors allege the marriages were part of an immigration scam; she faces up to four years in prison if convicted.

An Indiana pizzeria drew boycott calls and threats after its owners said they would not cater a same-sex wedding, intensifying debate over the state’s new religious freedom law. Supporters raised more than $842,000 for the family-run business, which closed temporarily after a threat to burn it down.

Mindy Kaling’s brother Vijay Chokalingam says he posed as Black on medical school applications to test whether affirmative action favored minority applicants. A CNN commentary argues that his single admission offer does little to support that claim and overlooks both the discrimination he experienced while posing as Black and the shortage of minority physicians.

A temperature of 63.5 degrees Fahrenheit (15.5 degrees Celsius) was recorded at an Argentine base in Antarctica on March 24, possibly a continental record. A World Meteorological Organization committee will review the measurement before an official finding, expected by late summer or early fall.

The United States has dropped its spring timetable for an Iraqi-led assault to retake Mosul from ISIS, saying no date has been set. Officials cited the need to build Iraqi forces’ capacity for an operation against a city of about one million people.

Irish bookmaker Paddy Power deleted a tweet comparing Newcastle’s losses at Liverpool with police beatings of unarmed African-American men after a social media backlash. The company said it was a joke and no offense was intended. Liverpool beat Newcastle 2-0 on Monday.

Philadelphia police added attempted murder to the charges against Nyia Parler, accused of leaving her quadriplegic son in woods for more than four days while she visited her boyfriend in Maryland. The 21-year-old was found dehydrated and malnourished. Parler remains in treatment in Maryland and cannot be extradited until it is complete.

A South Korean man accused of stabbing U.S. Ambassador Mark Lippert in Seoul has been charged with attempted murder and two other offenses. Lippert needed 80 stitches after the March 5 attack but was not expected to suffer permanent damage.
Jill (Duggar) Dillard of “19 Kids and Counting” gave birth Monday to a 9-pound, 10-ounce son, Israel David, People magazine reported. He is the first child for Dillard and her husband, Derick.

Universal’s “Furious 7” is projected to open to $135 million-$138 million in North America, the biggest debut since 2013. The final film featuring Paul Walker could approach or top $300 million worldwide by Easter Sunday.

A Secret Service supervisor has been placed on administrative leave and had his security clearance suspended after a female employee accused him of assault following unwanted sexual advances. The inspector general will investigate the allegation, the latest in a series of scandals at the agency.

Hillary Clinton is announcing her 2016 presidential bid as a formidable candidate whose poll standing has recently slipped. To win, she must offer a compelling agenda, connect with Democratic voters and address doubts about her authenticity, while navigating gender bias and potential liabilities involving her husband.

The Justice Department is preparing to negotiate reforms to Ferguson’s police department after finding widespread racial discrimination in policing and municipal courts. Voters have elected two Black city council members, and the police chief and city manager have resigned. The extent of further change will depend on residents’ influence over the reforms.

A cat traveling on an Etihad Airways flight from Abu Dhabi escaped after its carrier was damaged and remains missing nearly a week after arriving at New York’s JFK Airport. Etihad says it is investigating, helping search for Felix and reviewing its pet-handling procedures.

A container ship rescued Louis Jordan, 37, after he spent 66 days adrift off the Carolinas on a damaged sailboat. He survived on rainwater and fish after storms capsized the boat and broke its mast. Coast Guard officials said they had no reason to doubt his account.
